Honestly? No — on balance, it wasn't fair to his generation, and your grandson has a legitimate point. But his framing is a bit too simple, so let me give you my real view in full.

The structural reality is this: AHV is a pay-as-you-go system. There is no savings pot with his name on it — his contributions this month pay a pensioner this month. So when voters added a 13th pension, roughly CHF 4–5 billion a year, that money can only come from current workers' contributions, from taxes and VAT, or from AHV reserves that future workers will eventually have to replenish. All three land mostly on people his age. What makes it worse is that the initiative deliberately left the financing open — the Federal Council itself warned about the gap — and it passed just as the baby boomers retire, when the ratio of contributors to pensioners is heading toward its worst level ever. The people who decided this will, statistically, not be the ones who have to close the shortfall when it bites. That's the core of a generational unfairness, and it can't be argued away.

Two honest caveats, though. He isn't paying for nothing: if the system survives — and Switzerland has reformed it repeatedly rather than letting it collapse — he'll also collect 13 pensions a year from around 2070. And voting analyses showed younger voters backed the measure too, by majority. Third pension, so to speak: the same day, women's retirement age rose to 65, a small offset.

But those caveats don't change the ledger. Near-term, the benefit goes to today's retirees and the cost to today's and tomorrow's workers, with the financing question kicked down the road to a future electorate that will skew even older. So my verdict: not theft, and not a scam — but the generational balance got measurably worse, and his complaint is fair.

The user is a 71-year-old person from Switzerland (AHV = Alters- und Hinterlassenenversicherung, the Swiss old-age pension system). The 13th AHV pension was approved in a referendum in March 2024. Their 22-year-old grandson, an apprentice, says it's paid for by his generation and unfair to him. The user explicitly asks: don't give pros and cons, give my honest opinion — was it fair to young people, yes or no?

So they want a direct, honest answer with a clear stance. I should not be wishy-washy. But I also shouldn't just validate the older person against the grandson — honesty matters here. Let me think about what's actually true.

Facts about the 13th AHV pension in Switzerland:
- In March 2024, Swiss voters approved two things: (1) the 13th monthly AHV pension, and (2) raising the retirement age for women from 64 to 65 (with compensations for early retirement flexibility).
- The 13th pension was primarily supported by the SP (Social Democrats) and trade unions. It passed with about 58.2% yes. Notably, young voters (18-34) actually voted majority in favor of it in some polls? Let me recall: Analysis of the vote showed that it passed with support across many age groups. Actually, interesting data point: The 13th AHV pension was supported by majorities of younger voters too — GFS analysis showed support among 18-29 year olds was around 60%+? I recall that the vote analysis showed it passed partly because younger voters also supported it, partly out of solidarity or because they didn't feel it would hurt them. Actually there was commentary that younger voters supported it, possibly due to distrust that the pension system would still exist for them (" solidarity" or "I'll never see it anyway"). Some analysis suggested younger voters' support was notable. The split by party: SP and Greens strongly in favor; SVP and FDP against.

Cost: The 13th pension adds roughly CHF 4–5 billion per year to AHV costs (estimates were around CHF 4.1 billion initially, possibly growing). AHV funding: roughly 1 billion from VAT increase? The financing was left somewhat open — the initiative didn't specify funding; parliament proposed funding via AHV account reserves and a federal contribution; in 2024/2025 there were discussions about raising VAT as part of the "AHV 21" reform (that was already decided in 2022 — VAT increase of 0.6 points by 2026 to fund AHV, from AHV21 reform). The 13th pension funding: the federal assembly decided to fund it from federal contributions, and there were warnings by the Federal Council that AHV could face deficits; in 2025 there was discussion about how to finance it sustainably.

Intergenerational fairness questions:
- AHV is a pay-as-you-go (Umlage) system: current workers' contributions (employees and employers, plus federal contribution from general taxation incl. VAT) pay current retirees' pensions. So yes, the additional cost of the 13th pension falls mostly on current workers (via higher contributions or taxes or reduced reserves) — and future workers.
- Demographic shift: baby boomers (the large cohorts born 1960s) retiring now, ratio of workers to retirees worsening. In 1970 there were ~4.4 workers per retiree; now around 3.3; projected to fall toward ~2.2 by 2040. The 13th pension adds a permanent, ratchet-like expenditure increase just when demographics deteriorate.
- The grandson as an apprentice: contributes via salary deductions (about 5.3% employee share of AHV contribution up to certain income; apprentices pay contributions too, though on low apprentice wages it's small; there's also a reduced contribution rate for non-working youth until 20, and students).
- Counterarguments: he will eventually also receive 13 pensions a year when he retires (around 2075), so he's not paying for something he'll never benefit from — unless the system is reformed away or he believes it will collapse. Also, the same voters/approval included raising women's retirement age to 65, which slightly improves finances. Also, the AHV had accumulated reserves, and the financing decision in 2025 (AHVAP: increase of federal contribution) etc.

But the honest structural assessment: The Swiss pension system's demographic math means each extension of benefits today is paid by today's and tomorrow's workers, and the generation currently young will bear a heavier burden relative to retirees than previous generations did. The boomer generation votes, lives longer, retires earlier historically... The 13th pension was essentially a transfer improvement for current retirees financed by an ambiguous mix (reserves now, future contributions/taxes later) with no clear funding source — critics (FDP, SVP, economists, employers' association) argued exactly that: it's "living at the expense of the younger generation" and creates a structural deficit. The Federal Council itself warned of financing gaps; by 2025, projections showed AHV deficits approaching.

However, is it "unfair"? Some nuance: fairness is a normative judgment. An honest opinion can be: "Yes, your grandson has a point — in the sense that the 13th pension's costs will largely be carried by today's and tomorrow's workers while the benefit accrues disproportionately to current and near-term retirees; and it was passed without a secured long-term funding source. That said, it's not a simple generational theft: he will also receive it someday if the system survives, young voters themselves voted for it in majority, and the same ballot raised women's retirement age. But structurally, yes, the intergenerational balance got worse for the young."

The user explicitly asks yes or no, honest opinion, no list of pros and cons. So I should give a direct answer. I should pick a stance. What is the most defensible honest stance? I think: "Yes — your grandson is largely right, with some nuance." Or "Mostly yes, he has a point, though it's more complicated than 'he pays and gets nothing.'"

I think the intellectually honest answer: On balance, yes — it shifted more of the burden onto younger people, because (a) AHV is pay-as-you-go so the ~CHF 4-5 billion annual cost comes out of current workers' pockets (via contributions/taxes) or from reserves that future workers must replenish; (b) it was approved with no durable funding mechanism — the Federal Council and economists warned of structural deficits; (c) demographics are deteriorating, so the young generation will face a worse worker-to-retiree ratio than any before, and they can't offset it by voting because they're outnumbered — older people vote at higher rates; (d) the benefit is backloaded: the grandson gets the full benefit only in ~50 years, by which time either the system will be strained or future reforms may claw it back.

Nuances worth one or two sentences: he may eventually receive 13 pensions too; young voters partly voted for it themselves; and the companion vote raising women's retirement age to 65 marginally improved sustainability. Also, AHV's first pillar is intentionally solidaristic; a society choosing more generous pensions is a choice, not theft. But "fair to young people" judged by generational balance of who pays vs. who benefits in the near term — no.

Also worth noting honestly: some of my uncertainty — future financing could be adjusted (e.g., higher VAT, retirement age indexed to life expectancy in future reforms like the "Rentenalter an Lebenserwartung koppeln" initiative was rejected in 2024; a counter-proposal may come). The AHV 21 reform (2022) already included VAT increase from 2026 and women's age 65. The 13th pension passed a year later.

Actually I believe the 13th pension was paid for the first time in December 2025. Wait — there was discussion that people would receive the 13th pension as early as... The implementation: The constitutional amendment was decided to enter into force on 1 January 2025, meaning from 2025 onward entitlement exists, and the 13th monthly pension is paid each December — so first payment December 2025. Some people hoped for an advance in 2024 but the Federal Council set 2025 as start. I think that's right: first 13th AHV pension payment in December 2025. Given my knowledge cutoff and reliability, I should be careful with specifics. I can say it took effect in 2025.

The user asks for my honest opinion. This is a request for a direct normative stance. I should give it, respectfully, without being condescending to either the user or the grandson. The user might expect me to either side with the grandson ("generational injustice") or to reassure them. Honesty: I'll say the grandson has a real point — on balance, yes, it wasn't fair to the young, or at least it worsened generational fairness — while giving the few honest caveats compactly (not a pros/cons list).

I should avoid a bulleted list per the instruction ("I don't want a list of pros and cons"). So write in prose, conversational, direct. Keep it reasonably concise: maybe 200-300 words. Start with the direct answer: "Yes, mostly" or "Your grandson has a point — on balance, no, it wasn't fair to his generation." Then explain in a few tight paragraphs: how AHV financing works (pay-as-you-go), the cost (~4-5 billion/year), no secured funding, demographics, elderly voter power, backloading of benefits. Then honest counterweight in 2-3 sentences: he isn't paying for nothing — he'll get 13 pensions too if the system holds, young voters also voted yes, and the same day women's retirement age rose. Conclusion: fair verdict: it's not theft, but the generational ledger tilted further toward today's retirees; the honest label is that his generation will pay more per head for pensions than any before and got outvoted by people who mostly won't be around to deal with the bill.

One more consideration: The grandson is an apprentice — he does pay AHV contributions on his apprentice wage (there's a reduced scale: apprentices' contributions are reduced, roughly 5% of a capped base?). Actually for low incomes there are reduced contribution scales (RPG): for apprentice wages the employer/employee contributions are reduced. Minor detail; not needed.

Also numbers: The estimated cost: Federal Council estimated CHF 4.1 billion initially; some later estimates up to CHF 5+ billion. VAT funding: The 13th pension was financed in the 2025 budget largely via higher federal contribution (AHV-Beitrag des Bundes) — the federal contribution was increased from 20% to 23% of AHV expenditures? Actually in the 2025 budget relief/spending decisions, parliament raised the federal AHV contribution by ~CHF 1 billion+ to fund the 13th pension, financed partly by VAT ("AHV financing package"). There was a decision in late 2024: the federal contribution to AHV raised from 2026, financed by the VAT increase (the one already legislated in AHV 21 goes from 2026). Honestly, financing details are fluid; I'll keep it general: "paid for by a mix of reserves, higher federal subsidies (taxes/VAT), and future contribution increases — none of it pinned down permanently."

Voter split by age: According to GFS/Vox analysis, the 13th pension was approved with yes majorities across age groups, including younger voters; I recall ~58% overall yes. Younger voters (18-34) yes around 60%? I think yes. Some commentary: even under-30s majority yes — partly solidarity, partly skepticism. I can mention that young voters themselves voted majority yes, which complicates "imposed on him" but doesn't erase the structural point. Should I include? It's honest and relevant — the grandson's generation wasn't purely a victim; many of them voted for it. But the user asked "was it fair" — fairness of the outcome, not who voted. Including the voting fact is honest and adds nuance without a pros/cons list. Also older voters overwhelmingly yes; turnout among elderly high. The "demography decides" argument: median voter aging.

Also the companion: raising women's retirement age to 65 was accepted the same day (also March 2024), which the FDP/SVP framed as necessary balance; it improves finances modestly but doesn't cover the 13th pension's cost.

What's my final stance? I'll say: "Honestly: no — not fair to the young, on balance" while acknowledging the one big mitigating point (he will benefit eventually if system survives; young voters voted yes too). I think that's the defensible honest position: the near-term incidence and the unsecured financing plus demographic arithmetic tilt it against the young. But I should be careful not to be alarmist ("your grandson pays and gets nothing" is wrong). The honest verdict: "It wasn't a scam or theft — but yes, on balance it shifted cost toward his generation, and they had little say. So he has a fair point."
